title: Politics in India: Challenges to and Restoration of the Congress System

topics.title: The challenge of political succession: Nehru to Shastri to Indira

learn.hook: Many new democracies collapsed when their founding leader died. When Nehru died in May 1964, the world watched to see whether India would too.
points: Nehru died in May 1964. Many feared a crisis of succession, but the transition was smooth: Lal Bahadur Shastri was chosen unanimously as the leader of the Congress parliamentary party and became Prime Minister.
Shastri was Prime Minister from 1964 to 1966. He faced food shortages and the 1965 war with Pakistan, and gave the famous slogan 'Jai Jawan Jai Kisan'.

Shastri died suddenly at Tashkent in January 1966, soon after signing the Tashkent Agreement. The contest for leadership was between Morarji Desai and Indira Gandhi, and Indira Gandhi won in a secret ballot among Congress MPs, with more than two-thirds of their support.

The 'Syndicate' was an informal group of senior Congress leaders who controlled the party organisation. It was led by K. Kamaraj, Congress President, and included S.K. Patil, S. Nijalingappa, N. Sanjeeva Reddy and Atulya Ghosh.
The Syndicate played a key role in choosing both Shastri and Indira Gandhi, and expected Indira to depend on its advice.

example.q: Why was the succession after Nehru's death considered a test for Indian democracy?
steps: Nehru had dominated politics since independence.
Many newly independent countries had seen turmoil or military takeover after a founding leader's death.
India's smooth transfer of power to Shastri, and then to Indira Gandhi, showed that its democratic institutions worked.
example.answer: Because a smooth transfer of power without crisis proved democracy's strength

learn.reallife: 'Jai Jawan Jai Kisan' is still quoted on Republic Day and in farmer and soldier tributes across India.

topics.title: The fourth general election, 1967: a 'political earthquake'

learn.hook: In 1967 the Congress still won the Lok Sabha, but lost power in several states and saw many big leaders defeated. Observers called it a 'political earthquake'.
points: The period before 1967 was one of economic crisis: monsoon failure, widespread drought, a fall in agricultural production, serious food shortages, depletion of foreign exchange reserves, a drop in industrial production and exports, and higher military spending.
In June 1966 the government devalued the rupee, a step widely seen as taken under US pressure. Prices rose sharply, and protests spread.

Non-Congressism: Ram Manohar Lohia gave this strategy, arguing that the opposition parties should come together to defeat the Congress, which he saw as undemocratic and opposed to the interests of the poor.

Results of the 1967 election: the Congress got a majority in the Lok Sabha but with its lowest tally since 1952. Half the ministers in Indira Gandhi's cabinet and leaders like K. Kamaraj lost their seats. The Congress lost its majority in seven states, and in two more, defections prevented it from forming a government.
In Madras, the regional DMK came to power with a clear majority, helped by its leadership of the anti-Hindi agitation.

example.q: Give two economic reasons for the Congress's setback in 1967.
steps: Food shortages after drought and poor monsoons.
Devaluation of the rupee and rising prices; depletion of foreign exchange reserves.
example.answer: Food shortages and drought; devaluation and price rise

learn.reallife: Even today, inflation and farm distress can swing election results in Indian states, just as they did in 1967.

learn.hook: After 1967, parties that had little in common ideologically shared power in the states. And one MLA changed sides so often that he gave Indian politics a new phrase.
points: The 1967 elections brought coalition governments in many states. They were called Samyukta Vidhayak Dal (SVD) governments, meaning 'joint legislature party'.

These coalitions were ideologically varied. In Bihar the SVD government included the two socialist parties (SSP and PSP), the CPI on the left and the Jana Sangh on the right. In Punjab the 'Popular United Front' included the two rival Akali groups, the CPI, the CPI(M), the SSP, the Republican Party and the Jana Sangh.
Defection means an elected representative leaving the party on whose symbol he or she was elected and joining another party. Defections caused frequent rise and fall of state governments after 1967.
The phrase 'Aya Ram Gaya Ram' comes from Gaya Lal, an MLA in Haryana, who changed his party three times within a fortnight in 1967.
Defections were later checked by the anti-defection law, added to the Constitution in 1985.

example.q: Why were SVD governments in states unstable?
steps: They were coalitions of parties with very different ideologies.
Members often defected to other parties.
So disagreements and defections frequently brought them down.

learn.reallife: Debates about MLAs switching sides before a trust vote in today's state assemblies are linked to the 'Aya Ram Gaya Ram' politics that began in 1967.

topics.title: Indira Gandhi versus the Syndicate: the road to the split

learn.hook: In 1969 a sitting Prime Minister campaigned against her own party's official candidate for President, and won.
points: Indira Gandhi faced challenges from the Syndicate, which expected her to follow its advice. She gradually built her own independent position and tried to give the party a more radical, pro-poor image.

In 1967 the Congress Working Committee adopted a Ten-Point Programme, including social control of banks, nationalisation of general insurance, ceilings on urban property and income, public distribution of food grains, land reforms and house sites for the rural poor.
In 1969 President Zakir Hussain died. The Syndicate got N. Sanjeeva Reddy nominated as the official Congress candidate, despite Indira Gandhi's reservations.

Indira Gandhi encouraged the then Vice-President, V.V. Giri, to file his nomination as an independent. Just before the election she nationalised fourteen leading private banks (July 1969) and removed Morarji Desai as Finance Minister.
She called for a 'conscience vote', asking Congress MPs and MLAs to vote as they wished. V.V. Giri won, and the official Congress candidate lost.

example.q: Order these events of 1969: V.V. Giri elected President; Zakir Hussain dies; banks nationalised; Sanjeeva Reddy nominated.
steps: Zakir Hussain dies (May 1969).
Sanjeeva Reddy nominated as official candidate.
Fourteen banks nationalised (July 1969).
V.V. Giri elected President (August 1969).
example.answer: Zakir Hussain's death → Reddy nominated → banks nationalised → Giri elected

learn.reallife: Many public sector banks you see today, such as Bank of Baroda or Canara Bank, were among those nationalised in 1969.

topics.title: The Congress splits; privy purses abolished

learn.hook: By late 1969 the party that had led the freedom struggle had broken into two. One side was called the 'Organisation', the other the 'Requisitionists'.
points: The defeat of the official candidate formalised the split. The Congress President, S. Nijalingappa, expelled Indira Gandhi from the party in November 1969.
The Congress split into two: the Congress (O), for 'Organisation', led by the Syndicate, and the Congress (R), for 'Requisitionists', led by Indira Gandhi.
Indira Gandhi presented the split as an ideological fight between socialists and conservatives, the pro-poor and the pro-rich.
Privy purses were grants paid by the government to the former rulers of princely states and their heirs, promised at the time of integration. Indira Gandhi supported their abolition.

Her government's attempt to amend the Constitution in 1970 failed in the Rajya Sabha, and its order 'de-recognising' the princes was struck down by the Supreme Court. Privy purses were finally abolished by a constitutional amendment after the 1971 election.

example.q: Explain the meaning of Congress (O) and Congress (R).
steps: Congress (O): 'Organisation', the faction led by the Syndicate that controlled the party organisation.
Congress (R): 'Requisitionists', the faction led by Indira Gandhi.
The split came in 1969.

learn.reallife: Some former royal families still live in their palaces, but since 1971 they no longer receive privy purses from the government.

quiz.q: Assertion (A): The Congress split in 1969. Reason (R): The official Congress candidate lost the presidential election to a candidate backed by the Prime Minister.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both true; the election defeat formalised the split.
steps: A: true — the Congress split in 1969.
R: true — the official candidate lost to Giri, whom the PM backed.
R explains A: that defeat formalised the split.
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Privy purses were abolished before the 1971 election. Reason (R): The Supreme Court struck down the order de-recognising the princes.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: A is false: they were abolished after the 1971 election. R is true.
steps: A: false — privy purses ended by an amendment after the 1971 election.
R: true — the Supreme Court struck down the de-recognition order.
So A is false, but R is true.
Answer: A is false, but R is true

revise.summary: After the 1969 presidential poll, Nijalingappa expelled Indira Gandhi. The party split into Congress (O) and Congress (R). She called it socialists versus conservatives. Privy purses for ex-rulers were abolished only after the 1971 election.
remember: 1970 amendment failed in Rajya Sabha; Supreme Court struck down de-recognition
traps: Privy purses ended after, not before, the 1971 election

topics.title: The 1971 election and the restoration of Congress dominance

learn.hook: The opposition's slogan was 'Indira hatao'. Her reply was 'Garibi hatao'. In 1971 voters chose the second by a landslide.
points: Indira Gandhi recommended dissolving the Lok Sabha in December 1970, and fresh elections were held in February 1971, ahead of schedule.

The non-communist, non-Congress opposition parties, including the Congress (O), formed a 'Grand Alliance' with the slogan 'Indira hatao' (remove Indira). Indira Gandhi offered a positive programme with the slogan 'Garibi hatao' (remove poverty).
The Congress (R) and CPI alliance won more seats and votes than the Congress had won in any of the first four elections. The Congress (R) alone won 352 seats, while the Congress (O) won only 16.

Restoration: the Congress system was restored, but it was different. The new Congress depended heavily on the popularity of a single leader, Indira Gandhi, and had fewer factions and a weaker organisation.

The victory in the Bangladesh war in December 1971 further raised Indira Gandhi's popularity, and the Congress swept the state assembly elections of 1972. Exam tip: order the events of 1964-71 by date.

example.q: Compare the restored Congress of 1971 with the old Congress system.
steps: Old system: coalition of many groups and factions, strong organisation, internal opposition.
Restored Congress: dominance built around one popular leader, Indira Gandhi.
Fewer factions and less tolerance of internal opposition.
example.answer: The restored Congress depended on one leader rather than a broad coalition of factions

learn.reallife: Election slogans still matter in India: like 'Garibi hatao', a short catchy line can shape a whole campaign.

quiz.q: Indira Gandhi's slogan in the 1971 election was:
quiz.explain: 'Garibi hatao' meant remove poverty.
steps: Asked: Indira Gandhi's slogan in 1971.

'Indira hatao' was the opposition's slogan.
Answer: Garibi hatao

'Garibi hatao' was Indira Gandhi's own slogan.
Answer: Indira hatao

352 was the Congress (R) tally.

Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A

steps: A: true — the Congress (R) won a sweeping victory in 1971.

teach.praise: Hooray! 'Garibi hatao' beat 'Indira hatao', the Congress (R) won 352 seats, the Bangladesh victory added to her popularity, and Congress dominance returned around one leader!

revise.summary: In the early 1971 election, the Grand Alliance's 'Indira hatao' met Indira Gandhi's 'Garibi hatao'. The Congress (R) won 352 seats and the Congress (O) only 16. The restored Congress rested on one leader, helped further by the Bangladesh victory.
remember: Restored Congress: one leader, fewer factions, weaker organisation
traps: Do not swap the two slogans
